cards.name: product_rate_trend
cards.mechanism: For products the user bought in the window, compares how often the product appeared in the user's last 28 days of orders with how often it appeared in the 92 days before (smoothed log ratio), and also gives the earlier share on its own. A rising rate marks a habit that is forming. A high earlier share with a collapsed recent rate marks a lapsed staple: the user has switched away or stopped. Count- and decay-based features cannot separate a lapsed staple from a steady medium-frequency item.

cards.null_stratum: Candidates never bought in the window (no row), or users with all window orders inside the last 28 days: NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.product_id = c.product_id)

rival.explanation: The gain may simply be a window-restricted frequency (the user's share over the 120 days) that is less diluted by stale history than up_share.
rival.stratum: Users whose history before the 120-day window is long: (SELECT count(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = c.user_id) >= 8

cards.name: user_pace_shift
cards.mechanism: Captures the user's current ordering tempo. The acceleration column is the log ratio of the mean of the last two inter-order gaps to the user's median gap. The overdue column is the days since the last order divided by the median gap, which is robust to the outlier gaps that distort u_mean_gap. An accelerating user, or one placing the next order soon after the last, tends to place small top-ups that repeat the latest items. An overdue or slowing user tends to place a full restock with long-cycle items. These columns let the trees switch between those two regimes.
cards.stratum: Users with at least 4 orders in the window: (SELECT count(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.user_id) >= 4
cards.null_stratum: Users with at most one order in the window, where both columns are NULL: (SELECT count(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.user_id) <= 1
cards.sql: WITH o AS (SELECT user_id, order_id, ts, lag(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts, order_id) AS prev_ts, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts DESC, order_id DESC) AS rk FROM orders WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users)), g AS (SELECT user_id, rk, epoch(ts - prev_ts) / 86400.0 AS gap FROM o WHERE prev_ts IS NOT NULL), s AS (SELECT user_id, median(gap) AS med_gap, avg(gap) FILTER (WHERE rk <= 2) AS recent_gap FROM g GROUP BY user_id), lo AS (SELECT user_id, epoch(TIMESTAMP '{A}' - max(ts)) / 86400.0 AS dsl FROM orders WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users) GROUP BY user_id) SELECT lo.user_id, ln((s.recent_gap + 0.25) / (s.med_gap + 0.25)) AS f_x_c1_u_pace_accel, lo.dsl / (s.med_gap + 0.25) AS f_x_c1_u_overdue_med FROM lo LEFT JOIN s ON s.user_id = lo.user_id

twin.sql: WITH o AS (SELECT user_id, order_id, ts, lag(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts, order_id) AS prev_ts FROM orders WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users)), g AS (SELECT user_id, epoch(ts - prev_ts) / 86400.0 AS gap, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY hash(order_id), order_id) AS hr FROM o WHERE prev_ts IS NOT NULL), s AS (SELECT user_id, median(gap) AS med_gap, avg(gap) FILTER (WHERE hr <= 2) AS recent_gap, max(CASE WHEN hr = 1 THEN gap END) AS pseudo_gap FROM g GROUP BY user_id), lo AS (SELECT user_id FROM orders WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users) GROUP BY user_id) SELECT lo.user_id, ln((s.recent_gap + 0.25) / (s.med_gap + 0.25)) AS f_x_c1_u_pace_accel_tw, s.pseudo_gap / (s.med_gap + 0.25) AS f_x_c1_u_overdue_med_tw FROM lo LEFT JOIN s ON s.user_id = lo.user_id

rival.explanation: The median gap alone, a robust order frequency, may carry the gain as a cleaner version of u_mean_gap, independent of recency.
rival.stratum: Users with an irregular history, where one long pause inflates the mean gap: (SELECT count(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.user_id) >= 4

cards.name: topup_urgency
cards.mechanism: Measures how often the user bought the product in a top-up order, meaning one placed within 2 days of their previous order. The family gives the smoothed share of the user's product orders that were top-ups, plus the raw count. Products the user places an extra urgent order for are essentials they run out of or forgot. Such items reliably reappear in the next order, while products that only ride along in big restocks are less certain.
cards.stratum: Repeat candidates of users who placed at least one top-up order in the window: EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o1 JOIN orders o2 ON o1.user_id = o2.user_id AND o2.ts > o1.ts AND o2.ts < o1.ts + INTERVAL 2 DAY WHERE o1.user_id = c.user_id) AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.product_id = c.product_id)
cards.null_stratum: Users without any top-up order, where the share is a constant smoothing value: NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o1 JOIN orders o2 ON o1.user_id = o2.user_id AND o2.ts > o1.ts AND o2.ts < o1.ts + INTERVAL 2 DAY WHERE o1.user_id = c.user_id)
cards.sql: WITH o AS (SELECT user_id, order_id, ts, lag(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts, order_id) AS prev_ts FROM orders WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users)), ot AS (SELECT order_id, CASE WHEN prev_ts IS NOT NULL AND epoch(ts - prev_ts) < 172800 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS topup FROM o), up AS (SELECT DISTINCT l.user_id, l.product_id, l.order_id FROM lines l JOIN cand c ON c.user_id = l.user_id AND c.product_id = l.product_id) SELECT up.user_id, up.product_id, (sum(ot.topup) + 0.1) / (count(*) + 1.0) AS f_x_c1_up_topup_share, sum(ot.topup) AS f_x_c1_up_topup_cnt FROM up JOIN ot ON ot.order_id = up.order_id GROUP BY up.user_id, up.product_id

twin.sql: WITH ord AS (SELECT user_id, order_id, ts, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts, order_id) AS rn_t, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY hash(order_id), order_id) AS rn_h FROM orders WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users)), sh AS (SELECT a.user_id, a.order_id, b.ts FROM ord a JOIN ord b ON a.user_id = b.user_id AND a.rn_h = b.rn_t), o AS (SELECT user_id, order_id, ts, lag(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts, order_id) AS prev_ts FROM sh), ot AS (SELECT order_id, CASE WHEN prev_ts IS NOT NULL AND epoch(ts - prev_ts) < 172800 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS topup FROM o), up AS (SELECT DISTINCT l.user_id, l.product_id, l.order_id FROM lines l JOIN cand c ON c.user_id = l.user_id AND c.product_id = l.product_id) SELECT up.user_id, up.product_id, (sum(ot.topup) + 0.1) / (count(*) + 1.0) AS f_x_c1_up_topup_share_tw, sum(ot.topup) AS f_x_c1_up_topup_cnt_tw FROM up JOIN ot ON ot.order_id = up.order_id GROUP BY up.user_id, up.product_id

rival.explanation: Top-up orders are small, so the family may only proxy for products bought in small baskets, which p_basket_context already captures at the item level.
rival.stratum: Users with a small mean basket: (SELECT avg(n) FROM (SELECT count(DISTINCT l.product_id) AS n FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id GROUP BY l.order_id) z) < 8

cards.name: next_dow_routine
cards.mechanism: Predicts the weekday of the user's next order as the weekday of the last order shifted by the rounded median inter-order gap. It then measures the smoothed log lift of the product's share among the user's past orders on that weekday over its share among all the user's orders. Weekend orders are often big family restocks and weekday orders are routine top-ups. Matching the product to the occasion the user is about to have should reorder repeat candidates.
cards.stratum: Repeat candidates of users with at least 6 orders in the window spread over at least 3 weekdays: (SELECT count(DISTINCT date_part('isodow', o.ts)) FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = c.user_id) >= 3 AND (SELECT count(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = c.user_id) >= 6
cards.null_stratum: Users who always order on the same weekday, where the lift is about 0: (SELECT count(DISTINCT date_part('isodow', o.ts)) FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = c.user_id) = 1
cards.sql: WITH o AS (SELECT user_id, order_id, ts, date_part('isodow', ts) AS dw, lag(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts, order_id) AS prev_ts, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts DESC, order_id DESC) AS rk FROM orders WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users)), u AS (SELECT user_id, max(CASE WHEN rk = 1 THEN dw END) AS last_dw, median(epoch(ts - prev_ts) / 86400.0) AS med_gap, count(*) AS n FROM o GROUP BY user_id), pd AS (SELECT user_id, n, (last_dw - 1 + CAST(round(COALESCE(med_gap, 7.0)) AS BIGINT)) % 7 + 1 AS pdw FROM u), ud AS (SELECT o.user_id, count(*) AS nd FROM o JOIN pd ON pd.user_id = o.user_id AND o.dw = pd.pdw GROUP BY o.user_id), up AS (SELECT l.user_id, l.product_id, count(DISTINCT l.order_id) AS cp, count(DISTINCT l.order_id) FILTER (WHERE o.dw = pd.pdw) AS cpd FROM lines l JOIN cand c ON c.user_id = l.user_id AND c.product_id = l.product_id JOIN o ON o.order_id = l.order_id JOIN pd ON pd.user_id = l.user_id GROUP BY l.user_id, l.product_id) SELECT up.user_id, up.product_id, ln(((up.cpd + 2.0 * up.cp / pd.n) / (COALESCE(ud.nd, 0) + 2.0)) / (up.cp * 1.0 / pd.n)) AS f_x_c1_up_dow_lift FROM up JOIN pd ON pd.user_id = up.user_id LEFT JOIN ud ON ud.user_id = up.user_id

twin.sql: WITH ord AS (SELECT user_id, order_id, ts, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts, order_id) AS rn_t, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY hash(order_id), order_id) AS rn_h FROM orders WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users)), sh AS (SELECT a.user_id, a.order_id, b.ts FROM ord a JOIN ord b ON a.user_id = b.user_id AND a.rn_h = b.rn_t), o AS (SELECT user_id, order_id, ts, date_part('isodow', ts) AS dw, lag(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts, order_id) AS prev_ts, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts DESC, order_id DESC) AS rk FROM sh), u AS (SELECT user_id, max(CASE WHEN rk = 1 THEN dw END) AS last_dw, median(epoch(ts - prev_ts) / 86400.0) AS med_gap, count(*) AS n FROM o GROUP BY user_id), pd AS (SELECT user_id, n, (last_dw - 1 + CAST(round(COALESCE(med_gap, 7.0)) AS BIGINT)) % 7 + 1 AS pdw FROM u), ud AS (SELECT o.user_id, count(*) AS nd FROM o JOIN pd ON pd.user_id = o.user_id AND o.dw = pd.pdw GROUP BY o.user_id), up AS (SELECT l.user_id, l.product_id, count(DISTINCT l.order_id) AS cp, count(DISTINCT l.order_id) FILTER (WHERE o.dw = pd.pdw) AS cpd FROM lines l JOIN cand c ON c.user_id = l.user_id AND c.product_id = l.product_id JOIN o ON o.order_id = l.order_id JOIN pd ON pd.user_id = l.user_id GROUP BY l.user_id, l.product_id) SELECT up.user_id, up.product_id, ln(((up.cpd + 2.0 * up.cp / pd.n) / (COALESCE(ud.nd, 0) + 2.0)) / (up.cp * 1.0 / pd.n)) AS f_x_c1_up_dow_lift_tw FROM up JOIN pd ON pd.user_id = up.user_id LEFT JOIN ud ON ud.user_id = up.user_id

rival.explanation: The predicted weekday often equals the weekday of the latest order, so the lift may just re-encode presence in recent orders (up_last5_share).
rival.stratum: Users with a weekly cadence, where the predicted weekday equals the last order's weekday: (SELECT count(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = c.user_id) >= 4

cards.name: product_cadence_shift
cards.mechanism: For products the user bought at least twice in the window, compares the latest repurchase gap with the user's median gap for the product (log ratio). It also gives the days since the last purchase divided by that latest gap, a dueness against the current cadence rather than the lifetime mean behind up_due. A shrinking latest gap shows the product is being consumed faster now, for example a new household need. A stretched one shows the habit is fading. Dueness against the current cadence should time the next purchase better.
cards.stratum: Pairs with at least 3 purchases in the window: (SELECT count(DISTINCT l.order_id) FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.product_id = c.product_id) >= 3
cards.null_stratum: Pairs bought at most once in the window (no row): (SELECT count(DISTINCT l.order_id) FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.product_id = c.product_id) <= 1
cards.sql: WITH p AS (SELECT DISTINCT l.user_id, l.product_id, l.order_id, l.ts FROM lines l JOIN cand c ON c.user_id = l.user_id AND c.product_id = l.product_id), g AS (SELECT user_id, product_id, ts, lag(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id, product_id ORDER BY ts, order_id) AS prev_ts, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id, product_id ORDER BY ts DESC, order_id DESC) AS rk FROM p), s AS (SELECT user_id, product_id, max(CASE WHEN rk = 1 THEN epoch(ts - prev_ts) / 86400.0 END) AS last_gap, median(epoch(ts - prev_ts) / 86400.0) AS med_gap, epoch(TIMESTAMP '{A}' - max(ts)) / 86400.0 AS dsl FROM g GROUP BY user_id, product_id) SELECT user_id, product_id, ln((last_gap + 0.5) / (med_gap + 0.5)) AS f_x_c1_up_last_gap_rel, dsl / (last_gap + 0.5) AS f_x_c1_up_since_last_gap FROM s WHERE last_gap IS NOT NULL

twin.sql: WITH p AS (SELECT DISTINCT l.user_id, l.product_id, l.order_id, l.ts FROM lines l JOIN cand c ON c.user_id = l.user_id AND c.product_id = l.product_id), g AS (SELECT user_id, product_id, order_id, ts, lag(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id, product_id ORDER BY ts, order_id) AS prev_ts FROM p), q AS (SELECT user_id, product_id, epoch(ts - prev_ts) / 86400.0 AS gap, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id, product_id ORDER BY hash(order_id), order_id) AS hr FROM g WHERE prev_ts IS NOT NULL), s AS (SELECT user_id, product_id, max(CASE WHEN hr = 1 THEN gap END) AS last_gap, median(gap) AS med_gap FROM q GROUP BY user_id, product_id), d AS (SELECT user_id, product_id, epoch(TIMESTAMP '{A}' - max(ts)) / 86400.0 AS dsl FROM p GROUP BY user_id, product_id) SELECT s.user_id, s.product_id, ln((s.last_gap + 0.5) / (s.med_gap + 0.5)) AS f_x_c1_up_last_gap_rel_tw, d.dsl / (s.last_gap + 0.5) AS f_x_c1_up_since_last_gap_tw FROM s JOIN d ON d.user_id = s.user_id AND d.product_id = s.product_id

rival.explanation: The gain may come from using a window median instead of the lifetime mean interval, a more robust dueness, rather than from the recency of the gap.
rival.stratum: Pairs with an outlier gap: (SELECT count(DISTINCT l.order_id) FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.product_id = c.product_id) >= 4

cards.name: product_sale_silence
cards.mechanism: Captures recency of the product's life on the platform. The first column is the days since its first sale in the 120-day window, which marks new launches whose adoption is just starting. The silence column is the days since its latest sale times its daily order rate, which is the number of sales expected during the current silence. A high silence for a usually busy product signals it is out of stock or delisted, which ends repeat interest no matter how loyal the user was.
cards.stratum: Products with a usual rate of at least one order a week that have not sold in the last 2 days: product_id IN (SELECT product_id FROM lines GROUP BY product_id HAVING count(DISTINCT order_id) >= 17 AND max(ts) < TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 2 DAY)
cards.null_stratum: Products that sell daily and sold in the last day: product_id IN (SELECT product_id FROM lines GROUP BY product_id HAVING max(ts) >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 1 DAY AND count(DISTINCT order_id) >= 120)
cards.sql: SELECT product_id, epoch(TIMESTAMP '{A}' - min(ts)) / 86400.0 AS f_x_c1_p_first_sold_days, (epoch(TIMESTAMP '{A}' - max(ts)) / 86400.0) * count(DISTINCT order_id) / 120.0 AS f_x_c1_p_silence FROM lines GROUP BY product_id

twin.sql: WITH sh AS (SELECT a.order_id, b.ts FROM (SELECT order_id, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY hash(order_id), order_id) AS rn FROM orders) a JOIN (SELECT ts, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY ts, order_id) AS rn FROM orders) b ON a.rn = b.rn) SELECT l.product_id, epoch(TIMESTAMP '{A}' - min(sh.ts)) / 86400.0 AS f_x_c1_p_first_sold_days_tw, (epoch(TIMESTAMP '{A}' - max(sh.ts)) / 86400.0) * count(DISTINCT l.order_id) / 120.0 AS f_x_c1_p_silence_tw FROM lines l JOIN sh ON sh.order_id = l.order_id GROUP BY l.product_id

rival.explanation: Silence may just be a smooth function of popularity (p_buyers_7 and p_buyers_28), so any gain is re-learned popularity, not availability.
rival.stratum: Low-popularity products where both popularity and silence are noisy: product_id IN (SELECT product_id FROM lines GROUP BY product_id HAVING count(DISTINCT order_id) < 10)

cards.name: category_exploration_burst
cards.mechanism: Counts how many distinct products of the candidate's category the user bought for the first time in the window during the last 28 days. It also gives that count as a share of the category products the user bought in those 28 days. A user who is actively trialing in a category is shopping around, so another not-yet-bought product of that category becomes more likely, and the old favourites less sure. A category with zero new products is in a settled, loyal phase.
cards.stratum: Candidates in a category where the user tried a new product in the last 28 days: EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY AND l.master_category_id = (SELECT min(l2.master_category_id) FROM lines l2 WHERE l2.product_id = c.product_id) AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lines l3 WHERE l3.user_id = l.user_id AND l3.product_id = l.product_id AND l3.ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY))
cards.null_stratum: Candidates in categories the user did not buy in the last 28 days (both columns 0): NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY AND l.master_category_id = (SELECT min(l2.master_category_id) FROM lines l2 WHERE l2.product_id = c.product_id))
cards.sql: WITH pc AS (SELECT l.product_id, min(l.master_category_id) AS cat FROM lines l WHERE l.master_category_id IS NOT NULL AND l.product_id IN (SELECT product_id FROM cand) GROUP BY l.product_id), fp AS (SELECT l.user_id, l.master_category_id AS cat, l.product_id, min(l.ts) AS first_ts, max(l.ts) AS last_ts FROM lines l WHERE l.master_category_id IS NOT NULL AND l.user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users) GROUP BY l.user_id, l.master_category_id, l.product_id), uc AS (SELECT user_id, cat, count(*) FILTER (WHERE first_ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY) AS n_new, count(*) FILTER (WHERE last_ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY) AS n_act FROM fp GROUP BY user_id, cat) SELECT c.user_id, c.product_id, CASE WHEN pc.cat IS NOT NULL THEN COALESCE(uc.n_new, 0) END AS f_x_c1_uc_new_prod_28, CASE WHEN pc.cat IS NOT NULL THEN COALESCE(uc.n_new, 0) / (COALESCE(uc.n_act, 0) + 1.0) END AS f_x_c1_uc_new_share_28 FROM cand c LEFT JOIN pc ON pc.product_id = c.product_id LEFT JOIN uc ON uc.user_id = c.user_id AND uc.cat = pc.cat

twin.sql: WITH ord AS (SELECT user_id, order_id, ts, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts, order_id) AS rn_t, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY hash(order_id), order_id) AS rn_h FROM orders WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users)), sh AS (SELECT a.user_id, a.order_id, b.ts FROM ord a JOIN ord b ON a.user_id = b.user_id AND a.rn_h = b.rn_t), pc AS (SELECT l.product_id, min(l.master_category_id) AS cat FROM lines l WHERE l.master_category_id IS NOT NULL AND l.product_id IN (SELECT product_id FROM cand) GROUP BY l.product_id), fp AS (SELECT l.user_id, l.master_category_id AS cat, l.product_id, min(sh.ts) AS first_ts, max(sh.ts) AS last_ts FROM lines l JOIN sh ON sh.order_id = l.order_id WHERE l.master_category_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY l.user_id, l.master_category_id, l.product_id), uc AS (SELECT user_id, cat, count(*) FILTER (WHERE first_ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY) AS n_new, count(*) FILTER (WHERE last_ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY) AS n_act FROM fp GROUP BY user_id, cat) SELECT c.user_id, c.product_id, CASE WHEN pc.cat IS NOT NULL THEN COALESCE(uc.n_new, 0) END AS f_x_c1_uc_new_prod_28_tw, CASE WHEN pc.cat IS NOT NULL THEN COALESCE(uc.n_new, 0) / (COALESCE(uc.n_act, 0) + 1.0) END AS f_x_c1_uc_new_share_28_tw FROM cand c LEFT JOIN pc ON pc.product_id = c.product_id LEFT JOIN uc ON uc.user_id = c.user_id AND uc.cat = pc.cat

rival.explanation: The count of new products may reflect how wide the category is (many substitutes), not the user's current exploration, so the gain would come from category breadth.
rival.stratum: Large categories with many distinct products: (SELECT count(DISTINCT l.product_id) FROM lines l WHERE l.master_category_id = (SELECT min(l2.master_category_id) FROM lines l2 WHERE l2.product_id = c.product_id)) >= 200

cards.name: item_freshness_availability
cards.mechanism: Life-cycle stage of the product. Age is the number of days since its first sale in the visible 120-day window, so recent launches stand apart from established assortment. Availability continuity is the share of days in the last 28 (or since launch, if younger) with at least one sale. A newly launched product draws trial from users who have not bought it yet. A product with broken day coverage is intermittently stocked or being phased out, so a user is less likely to find and add it in the next order even when popularity counts look fine.
cards.stratum: Candidates that are recent launches or intermittently sold tail products: (SELECT min(l.ts) FROM lines l WHERE l.product_id = c.product_id AND l.ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}') >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 42 DAY OR (SELECT count(DISTINCT CAST(l.ts AS DATE)) FROM lines l WHERE l.product_id = c.product_id AND l.ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY AND l.ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}') < 20
cards.null_stratum: Staples sold every day for the whole window, where both columns saturate: (SELECT count(DISTINCT CAST(l.ts AS DATE)) FROM lines l WHERE l.product_id = c.product_id AND l.ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY AND l.ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}') = 28 AND (SELECT min(l.ts) FROM lines l WHERE l.product_id = c.product_id AND l.ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}') < TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 110 DAY
cards.sql: WITH p AS (SELECT product_id, min(ts) AS first_ts, count(DISTINCT CAST(ts AS DATE)) FILTER (WHERE ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY) AS sale_days28 FROM lines WHERE ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}' GROUP BY product_id) SELECT product_id, epoch(TIMESTAMP '{A}' - first_ts) / 86400.0 AS f_x_c2_p_age_days, LEAST(1.0, sale_days28 / LEAST(28.0, GREATEST(1.0, epoch(TIMESTAMP '{A}' - first_ts) / 86400.0))) AS f_x_c2_p_avail_days_share FROM p

twin.sql: WITH l AS (SELECT product_id, CAST(hash(order_id) % 120 AS DOUBLE) + 0.5 AS age_d FROM lines WHERE ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}'), p AS (SELECT product_id, max(age_d) AS age_max, count(DISTINCT floor(age_d)) FILTER (WHERE age_d < 28) AS sale_days28 FROM l GROUP BY product_id) SELECT product_id, age_max AS f_x_c2_p_age_days_tw, LEAST(1.0, sale_days28 / LEAST(28.0, GREATEST(1.0, age_max))) AS f_x_c2_p_avail_days_share_tw FROM p

rival.explanation: Availability share is a smoothed proxy of low-volume popularity: it helps only by refining p_buyers_28 for tail products, not through life-cycle or stock effects.
rival.stratum: Tail candidates with p_buyers_28 below 20, regardless of age or launch date

cards.name: item_audience_growth_curve
cards.mechanism: Growth and decay of the product audience, measured as the share of active buyers rather than raw counts, so that anchor-to-anchor swings in total traffic cancel. The first column is the log-linear slope of the weekly buyer share over the last 8 weeks. The second is the log of the latest 14-day block's buyer share relative to the product's peak 14-day block over 112 days. Rising products should gain adopters and repeaters in the next 14 days. Products far below their own peak (spent promotions, faded fads, seasonal tails) should lose them. Both effects are smoother and longer-range than the 7/28 ratio in p_trend.
cards.stratum: Candidates whose audience moved strongly over two months, e.g. weekly buyers in the last 14 days differ from those in [A-56, A-42) by more than 50 percent: abs(ln((1.0 + (SELECT count(DISTINCT l.user_id) FROM lines l WHERE l.product_id = c.product_id AND l.ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 14 DAY AND l.ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}')) / (1.0 + (SELECT count(DISTINCT l.user_id) FROM lines l WHERE l.product_id = c.product_id AND l.ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 56 DAY AND l.ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 42 DAY)))) > 0.4
cards.null_stratum: Products with a flat audience: the same expression <= 0.1
cards.sql: WITH lw AS (SELECT product_id, user_id, CAST(floor(epoch(TIMESTAMP '{A}' - ts) / 604800) AS INTEGER) AS wk FROM lines WHERE ts > TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 112 DAY AND ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}'), actw AS (SELECT wk, count(DISTINCT user_id) AS n_act FROM lw WHERE wk < 8 GROUP BY wk), actf AS (SELECT wk // 2 AS fn, count(DISTINCT user_id) AS n_act FROM lw GROUP BY wk // 2), pw AS (SELECT product_id, wk, count(DISTINCT user_id) AS nb FROM lw WHERE wk < 8 GROUP BY product_id, wk), pf AS (SELECT product_id, wk // 2 AS fn, count(DISTINCT user_id) AS nb FROM lw GROUP BY product_id, wk // 2), pr AS (SELECT DISTINCT product_id FROM lw), sl AS (SELECT pr.product_id, regr_slope(ln((COALESCE(pw.nb, 0) + 0.5) / a.n_act), -1.0 * a.wk) AS slope FROM pr CROSS JOIN actw a LEFT JOIN pw ON pw.product_id = pr.product_id AND pw.wk = a.wk GROUP BY pr.product_id), pk AS (SELECT pr.product_id, max(CASE WHEN a.fn = 0 THEN (COALESCE(pf.nb, 0) + 0.5) / a.n_act END) / max((COALESCE(pf.nb, 0) + 0.5) / a.n_act) AS peak FROM pr CROSS JOIN actf a LEFT JOIN pf ON pf.product_id = pr.product_id AND pf.fn = a.fn GROUP BY pr.product_id) SELECT sl.product_id, sl.slope AS f_x_c2_p_share_slope8w, ln(pk.peak) AS f_x_c2_p_peak_ratio FROM sl JOIN pk ON pk.product_id = sl.product_id

cards.name: item_habit_abandonment
cards.mechanism: Decay of a product's audience, measured only among buyers who are still active. Among users who bought the product in [A-120, A-28) and placed at least one order in [A-28, A), it is the smoothed share who did not buy it again in [A-28, A). The second column restricts this to habitual buyers (2+ earlier orders with the product). Conditioning on activity makes the rate robust to traffic shifts between anchors: users who churned or paused do not count as abandoning. A high habitual abandonment rate flags delisting, quality or price problems, or substitution by a new variant, which should lower the repeat chance of the user's own history with the product.
cards.stratum: Repeat candidates of active users that were bought at least twice before A-28: (SELECT count(DISTINCT l.order_id) FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.product_id = c.product_id AND l.ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY) >= 2
cards.null_stratum: Candidates never bought by the user before A-28 (adoption candidates from sources b and c): NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.product_id = c.product_id AND l.ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY)

rival.stratum: All repeat candidates equally, with the gain concentrated on low-repeat impulse categories rather than on recently delisted items

cards.name: retailer_supply_silence
cards.mechanism: Availability decay of the product at the user's main retailer, approximated over the 120-day window. The first column is the days since the product last sold there, times its usual sale-day frequency over the last 28 days, which gives the number of expected sale days that passed without a sale. A daily seller silent for several days is likely out of stock or delisted. The second column is the share of the last 14 days with a sale there. Next-order purchases require the product to be on the shelf of the retailer the user shops at. These columns should demote repeat candidates the user can no longer get, and promote items that are reliably stocked where the user shops.
cards.stratum: User x item pairs where the product sold at the retailer of the user's latest order in [A-28, A-7) but not in [A-7, A): EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lines l JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = l.order_id WHERE l.product_id = c.product_id AND o.retailer = (SELECT arg_max(o2.retailer, o2.ts) FROM orders o2 WHERE o2.user_id = c.user_id AND o2.ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}') AND l.ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY AND l.ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 7 DAY) AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lines l JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = l.order_id WHERE l.product_id = c.product_id AND o.retailer = (SELECT arg_max(o2.retailer, o2.ts) FROM orders o2 WHERE o2.user_id = c.user_id AND o2.ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}') AND l.ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 7 DAY AND l.ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}')
cards.null_stratum: Pairs whose product sold at that retailer on at least 12 of the last 14 days (continuously stocked): (SELECT count(DISTINCT CAST(l.ts AS DATE)) FROM lines l JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = l.order_id WHERE l.product_id = c.product_id AND o.retailer = (SELECT arg_max(o2.retailer, o2.ts) FROM orders o2 WHERE o2.user_id = c.user_id AND o2.ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}') AND l.ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 14 DAY AND l.ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}') >= 12
cards.sql: WITH uo AS (SELECT o.user_id, o.retailer, count(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS n_ord, max(o.ts) AS last_ts FROM orders o JOIN users u ON u.user_id = o.user_id WHERE o.ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}' GROUP BY o.user_id, o.retailer), mr AS (SELECT user_id, retailer FROM (SELECT user_id, retailer, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY n_ord DESC, last_ts DESC, retailer) AS rn FROM uo) WHERE rn = 1), rp AS (SELECT o.retailer, l.product_id, max(l.ts) AS last_ts, count(DISTINCT CAST(l.ts AS DATE)) FILTER (WHERE l.ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY) AS sd28, count(DISTINCT CAST(l.ts AS DATE)) FILTER (WHERE l.ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 14 DAY) AS sd14 FROM lines l JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = l.order_id WHERE l.ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}' AND o.retailer IN (SELECT retailer FROM mr) AND l.product_id IN (SELECT product_id FROM cand) GROUP BY o.retailer, l.product_id) SELECT c.user_id, c.product_id, CASE WHEN mr.retailer IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE COALESCE(epoch(TIMESTAMP '{A}' - rp.last_ts) / 86400.0 * GREATEST(rp.sd28, 1) / 28.0, 5.0) END AS f_x_c2_pr_silence_rel, CASE WHEN mr.retailer IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE COALESCE(rp.sd14, 0) / 14.0 END AS f_x_c2_pr_sale_days14 FROM cand c LEFT JOIN mr ON mr.user_id = c.user_id LEFT JOIN rp ON rp.retailer = mr.retailer AND rp.product_id = c.product_id

rival.explanation: Sale-day coverage at the retailer is a saturating transform of p_buyers_28_main, so any gain is retailer popularity, not stock-outs.
rival.stratum: Low-popularity repeat candidates at small retailers, with no dependence on recent silence

cards.name: upcoming_weekday_fit
cards.mechanism: Weekly rhythm. Each order's weekday is taken relative to the anchor (days to A modulo 7), and the user's weekday distribution is decayed by how far that weekday lies after A. This approximates the weekday of the user's first order in [A, A+14). The first column is the log of the product's weekday lift (its share of orders on that weekday versus all orders) averaged under this distribution, e.g. weekend-party, Monday-restock or Friday-alcohol items. The second column is the user's own share of orders containing the product on those upcoming weekdays, relative to the user's overall share. A habitual weekend-only purchase should rank higher when the next likely order falls on that weekday.
cards.stratum: Users with a concentrated weekday habit (at least 60 percent of orders on one relative weekday, at least 5 orders) x products bought by them: (SELECT max(cnt) * 1.0 / sum(cnt) FROM (SELECT date_diff('day', o.ts, TIMESTAMP '{A}') % 7 AS rd, count(*) AS cnt FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = c.user_id AND o.ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}' GROUP BY date_diff('day', o.ts, TIMESTAMP '{A}') % 7)) >= 0.6 AND (SELECT count(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = c.user_id AND o.ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}') >= 5
cards.null_stratum: Users whose orders spread evenly over the week (max relative-weekday share <= 0.25), where the weekday expectation is flat

cards.name: hour_band_fit
cards.mechanism: Daily rhythm. Orders are split into six 4-hour bands. The user's habitual band is a recency-weighted distribution over orders with weight exp(-age/28 days), and it is stable from order to order. The column is the log of the product's lift in those bands relative to all orders: breakfast and fresh items in morning orders, snacks and drinks in evening orders. Among popular candidates the user never bought, this promotes those matching the time of day the user shops. The next order will most likely be placed in the same band.
cards.stratum: Users with a concentrated hour habit (at least 70 percent of orders in one 4-hour band, at least 4 orders) x candidates the user never bought: NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.product_id = c.product_id AND l.ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}') AND (SELECT max(cnt) * 1.0 / sum(cnt) FROM (SELECT hour(o.ts) // 4 AS hb, count(*) AS cnt FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = c.user_id AND o.ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}' GROUP BY hour(o.ts) // 4)) >= 0.7
cards.null_stratum: Users whose orders spread across bands (max band share <= 0.35), where the expectation is close to the global mix
cards.sql: WITH oh AS (SELECT order_id, user_id, ts, hour(ts) // 4 AS hb FROM orders WHERE ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}'), tot AS (SELECT hb, count(*) / sum(count(*)) OVER () AS s_hb FROM oh GROUP BY hb), ph AS (SELECT l.product_id, oh.hb, count(DISTINCT l.order_id) AS n FROM lines l JOIN oh ON oh.order_id = l.order_id WHERE l.product_id IN (SELECT product_id FROM cand) GROUP BY l.product_id, oh.hb), pt AS (SELECT product_id, sum(n) AS n_p FROM ph GROUP BY product_id), plift AS (SELECT pt.product_id, tot.hb, ((COALESCE(ph.n, 0) + 5 * tot.s_hb) / (pt.n_p + 5)) / tot.s_hb AS lf FROM pt CROSS JOIN tot LEFT JOIN ph ON ph.product_id = pt.product_id AND ph.hb = tot.hb), uh AS (SELECT oh.user_id, oh.hb, sum(exp(-epoch(TIMESTAMP '{A}' - oh.ts) / 86400.0 / 28.0)) AS wt FROM oh JOIN users u ON u.user_id = oh.user_id GROUP BY oh.user_id, oh.hb), uv AS (SELECT user_id, hb, wt / sum(wt) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id) AS v FROM uh) SELECT c.user_id, c.product_id, ln(sum(uv.v * plift.lf)) AS f_x_c2_up_hour_lift FROM cand c JOIN uv ON uv.user_id = c.user_id JOIN plift ON plift.product_id = c.product_id AND plift.hb = uv.hb GROUP BY c.user_id, c.product_id

cards.name: item_trial_conversion
cards.mechanism: Trial-to-habit transition in the product life cycle. A trial is a user's first purchase of the product in the window, counted only when the user had been ordering for at least 28 days before it, to limit left-truncation. The first column is the smoothed share of trials followed by another purchase of the product within 28 days. The second is the conversion of the recent trial cohort ([A-56, A-28)) minus that of the older cohort. A falling difference marks a novelty that no longer converts, a rising one a product settling into baskets. This applies directly to the many candidates the user bought exactly once, and to adoption candidates.
cards.stratum: Pairs where the user bought the product in exactly one order before A: (SELECT count(DISTINCT l.order_id) FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.product_id = c.product_id AND l.ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}') = 1
cards.null_stratum: Long-established habits of the user (5+ orders with the product), where trial behaviour is irrelevant: (SELECT count(DISTINCT l.order_id) FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.product_id = c.product_id AND l.ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}') >= 5
cards.sql: WITH up AS (SELECT DISTINCT user_id, product_id, order_id, ts FROM lines WHERE ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}'), f AS (SELECT user_id, product_id, min(ts) AS first_ts FROM up GROUP BY user_id, product_id), uf AS (SELECT user_id, min(ts) AS ufirst_ts FROM orders WHERE ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}' GROUP BY user_id), tr AS (SELECT f.product_id, f.first_ts, max(CASE WHEN up.ts > f.first_ts AND up.ts <= f.first_ts + INTERVAL 28 DAY THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS conv FROM f JOIN uf ON uf.user_id = f.user_id JOIN up ON up.user_id = f.user_id AND up.product_id = f.product_id WHERE f.first_ts <= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY AND uf.ufirst_ts <= f.first_ts - INTERVAL 28 DAY GROUP BY f.user_id, f.product_id, f.first_ts), g AS (SELECT avg(conv) AS g_all FROM tr), pp AS (SELECT tr.product_id, (sum(tr.conv) + 20 * g.g_all) / (count(*) + 20) AS p_all, sum(tr.conv) FILTER (WHERE tr.first_ts > TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 56 DAY) AS s_new, count(*) FILTER (WHERE tr.first_ts > TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 56 DAY) AS n_new, sum(tr.conv) FILTER (WHERE tr.first_ts <= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 56 DAY) AS s_old, count(*) FILTER (WHERE tr.first_ts <= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 56 DAY) AS n_old FROM tr CROSS JOIN g GROUP BY tr.product_id, g.g_all) SELECT product_id, p_all AS f_x_c2_p_trial_conv28, (COALESCE(s_new, 0) + 10 * p_all) / (n_new + 10) - (COALESCE(s_old, 0) + 10 * p_all) / (n_old + 10) AS f_x_c2_p_trial_conv_shift FROM pp

rival.explanation: Trial conversion is mainly a restatement of the product's general repurchase rate (ag_p_next_reorder, ag_p_rebuy14), so any gain is a better-smoothed staple score rather than a trial-specific life-cycle signal.
rival.stratum: All repeat candidates, including those bought many times, with no concentration on single-purchase pairs

cards.name: item_weekly_overdispersion
cards.mechanism: Robustness of a product's popularity to short-lived shifts. The value is the Pearson overdispersion of its weekly distinct-buyer counts over the last 8 weeks against the counts expected from each week's active-user traffic: (sum (n_w - e_w)^2 / e_w) / 7, logged. Poisson noise gives about 1 at any popularity level, so the value measures bursts rather than volume. Spiky products (one-off promotions, events) get pop-retailer and global ranks inflated by a temporary buyer wave that will not carry into the next 14 days. Steady products have reliable ranks. This lets the model discount source b and c ranks for bursty items.
cards.stratum: Candidates from the popularity sources that the user never bought and that had one week with more than twice their mean weekly buyers in the last 8 weeks: NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.product_id = c.product_id AND l.ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}') AND (SELECT max(nb) / avg(nb) FROM (SELECT floor(epoch(TIMESTAMP '{A}' - l.ts) / 604800) AS wk, count(DISTINCT l.user_id) AS nb FROM lines l WHERE l.product_id = c.product_id AND l.ts > TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 56 DAY AND l.ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}' GROUP BY floor(epoch(TIMESTAMP '{A}' - l.ts) / 604800))) > 2
cards.null_stratum: Repeat candidates with at least 3 orders by the user, where the user's own history dominates popularity ranks: (SELECT count(DISTINCT l.order_id) FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.product_id = c.product_id AND l.ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}') >= 3
cards.sql: WITH lw AS (SELECT product_id, user_id, CAST(floor(epoch(TIMESTAMP '{A}' - ts) / 604800) AS INTEGER) AS wk FROM lines WHERE ts > TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 56 DAY AND ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}'), act AS (SELECT wk, count(DISTINCT user_id) AS n_act FROM lw GROUP BY wk), allact AS (SELECT sum(n_act) AS n_act_all FROM act), pw AS (SELECT product_id, wk, count(DISTINCT user_id) AS nb FROM lw GROUP BY product_id, wk), pr AS (SELECT product_id, sum(nb) AS n_tot FROM pw GROUP BY product_id), s AS (SELECT pr.product_id, COALESCE(pw.nb, 0) AS nb, pr.n_tot * a.n_act / allact.n_act_all AS e FROM pr CROSS JOIN act a CROSS JOIN allact LEFT JOIN pw ON pw.product_id = pr.product_id AND pw.wk = a.wk) SELECT product_id, ln(sum((nb - e) * (nb - e) / e) / 7.0 + 0.1) AS f_x_c2_p_week_overdisp FROM s GROUP BY product_id

twin.sql: WITH lw AS (SELECT product_id, user_id, CAST(hash(order_id) % 8 AS INTEGER) AS wk FROM lines WHERE ts > TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 56 DAY AND ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}'), act AS (SELECT wk, count(DISTINCT user_id) AS n_act FROM lw GROUP BY wk), allact AS (SELECT sum(n_act) AS n_act_all FROM act), pw AS (SELECT product_id, wk, count(DISTINCT user_id) AS nb FROM lw GROUP BY product_id, wk), pr AS (SELECT product_id, sum(nb) AS n_tot FROM pw GROUP BY product_id), s AS (SELECT pr.product_id, COALESCE(pw.nb, 0) AS nb, pr.n_tot * a.n_act / allact.n_act_all AS e FROM pr CROSS JOIN act a CROSS JOIN allact LEFT JOIN pw ON pw.product_id = pr.product_id AND pw.wk = a.wk) SELECT product_id, ln(sum((nb - e) * (nb - e) / e) / 7.0 + 0.1) AS f_x_c2_p_week_overdisp_tw FROM s GROUP BY product_id

rival.explanation: Overdispersion grows with volume for popular products, because fixed weekly fluctuations are large in Poisson units. The column then acts as a monotone popularity proxy duplicating glob_rank.
rival.stratum: Top glob_rank candidates (glob_rank <= 100), with no extra gain on spiky tail items

cards.name: seed_cooc_pmi
cards.mechanism: Measures how strongly the candidate co-occurs in shoppers' baskets with the user's core repertoire. The repertoire is the user's top-10 products by distinct orders in the 120-day window, weighted by that count. The co-occurrence graph is built over the last 14 days of all orders. Two columns: the seed-weighted mean of P(candidate in order | seed in order), and the log of the seed-weighted lift n_co*N/(n_seed*n_cand). Complements of a user's staples (pasta with sauce, cereal with milk) are likely to enter the next basket. The existing last_order_copurchase uses only the latest order as seeds. This card uses the stable repertoire, so it scores complements of habitual items even when the last order was a small top-up.
cards.stratum: Candidates the user has not bought, for users with at least 3 orders in the window. Predicate: NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.product_id = c.product_id) AND (SELECT count(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = c.user_id) >= 3
cards.null_stratum: Long-standing repeat candidates, where the user's own frequency dominates. Predicate: (SELECT count(DISTINCT l.order_id) FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.product_id = c.product_id) >= 5

hash(product_id), product_id)) AS sub_id FROM pb), seeds_tw AS (SELECT s.user_id, pm.sub_id AS seed_id, s.n_ord, pq.n_p AS n_q FROM seeds s JOIN perm pm ON pm.product_id = s.seed_id JOIN pcnt pq ON pq.product_id = pm.sub_id), co AS (SELECT a.product_id AS seed_id, b.product_id, count(*) AS n_co FROM ol a JOIN ol b ON a.order_id = b.order_id AND a.product_id <> b.product_id WHERE a.product_id IN (SELECT seed_id FROM seeds_tw) AND b.product_id IN (SELECT product_id FROM cand) GROUP BY a.product_id, b.product_id) SELECT c.user_id, c.product_id, sum(s.n_ord * COALESCE(co.n_co, 0) / s.n_q) / sum(s.n_ord) AS f_x_c3_seed_cooc_cond_tw, ln(1 + sum(s.n_ord * COALESCE(co.n_co, 0) * CAST(n.n_all AS DOUBLE) / (s.n_q * COALESCE(pc.n_p, 1))) / sum(s.n_ord)) AS f_x_c3_seed_cooc_lift_tw FROM cand c JOIN seeds_tw s ON s.user_id = c.user_id AND s.seed_id <> c.product_id LEFT JOIN co ON co.seed_id = s.seed_id AND co.product_id = c.product_id LEFT JOIN pcnt pc ON pc.product_id = c.product_id CROSS JOIN nall n GROUP BY c.user_id, c.product_id

rival.explanation: The co-occurrence mean mostly re-encodes candidate popularity among shoppers of mainstream seeds, or category affinity, not specific complementarity.
rival.stratum: Top-popularity candidates (glob_rank <= 100), and candidates in the user's most frequent categories

cards.name: next_order_addition_transition
cards.mechanism: A cross-user sequential transition graph over consecutive orders of the same user. Each next order falls in the last 28 days. For each product q in the previous order, it counts the products p that were added in the next order, meaning present in the next order but absent from the previous one. Seeds are the products of the user's latest order, excluding the candidate itself. The columns are the mean smoothed P(p added next | q in previous) and its log lift over p's base addition rate. This captures order-to-order dynamics: what people buy the order after buying X (e.g. replenishment chains, alternating product lines). It differs from same-basket co-occurrence (last_order_copurchase) and from self-reorder rates.
cards.stratum: Candidates absent from the user's latest order. Predicate: NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.product_id = c.product_id AND l.ts = (SELECT max(o.ts) AS last_ts FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = c.user_id))
cards.null_stratum: Candidates contained in the user's latest order. An addition is impossible there by construction, so the value only reflects other seeds. Predicate: EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.product_id = c.product_id AND l.ts = (SELECT max(o.ts) AS last_ts FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = c.user_id))
cards.sql: WITH ord AS (SELECT order_id, user_id, ts, lag(order_id) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts, order_id) AS prev_order_id FROM orders), tr AS (SELECT order_id, prev_order_id FROM ord WHERE prev_order_id IS NOT NULL AND ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY), ol AS (SELECT DISTINCT order_id, product_id FROM lines), ntr AS (SELECT count(*) AS n_tr FROM tr), lastord AS (SELECT user_id, order_id FROM (SELECT user_id, order_id, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts DESC, order_id DESC) AS rn FROM orders WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users)) x WHERE rn = 1), seeds AS (SELECT DISTINCT lo.user_id, ol.product_id AS seed_id FROM lastord lo JOIN ol ON ol.order_id = lo.order_id), prevp AS (SELECT tr.order_id, ol.product_id FROM tr JOIN ol ON ol.order_id = tr.prev_order_id), added AS (SELECT nl.order_id, nl.product_id FROM tr JOIN ol nl ON nl.order_id = tr.order_id LEFT JOIN prevp p ON p.order_id = nl.order_id AND p.product_id = nl.product_id WHERE p.order_id IS NULL), padd AS (SELECT product_id, count(*) AS n_add FROM added WHERE product_id IN (SELECT product_id FROM cand) GROUP BY product_id), qn AS (SELECT product_id AS seed_id, count(*) AS n_q FROM prevp WHERE product_id IN (SELECT seed_id FROM seeds) GROUP BY product_id), qp AS (SELECT p.product_id AS seed_id, a.product_id, count(*) AS n_qp FROM prevp p JOIN added a ON a.order_id = p.order_id WHERE p.product_id IN (SELECT seed_id FROM seeds) AND a.product_id IN (SELECT product_id FROM cand) GROUP BY p.product_id, a.product_id), sc AS (SELECT c.user_id, c.product_id, avg(COALESCE(qp.n_qp, 0) / (qn.n_q + 5.0)) AS p_add FROM cand c JOIN seeds s ON s.user_id = c.user_id AND s.seed_id <> c.product_id JOIN qn ON qn.seed_id = s.seed_id LEFT JOIN qp ON qp.seed_id = s.seed_id AND qp.product_id = c.product_id GROUP BY c.user_id, c.product_id) SELECT sc.user_id, sc.product_id, sc.p_add AS f_x_c3_next_add_prob, ln((sc.p_add + 0.0001) / ((COALESCE(pa.n_add, 0) + 1.0) / (n.n_tr + 1.0) + 0.0001)) AS f_x_c3_next_add_lift FROM sc LEFT JOIN padd pa ON pa.product_id = sc.product_id CROSS JOIN ntr n

INTERVAL 28 DAY), ol AS (SELECT DISTINCT order_id, product_id FROM lines), ntr AS (SELECT count(*) AS n_tr FROM tr), lastord AS (SELECT user_id, order_id FROM (SELECT user_id, order_id, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts DESC, order_id DESC) AS rn FROM orders WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users)) x WHERE rn = 1), seeds AS (SELECT DISTINCT lo.user_id, ol.product_id AS seed_id FROM lastord lo JOIN ol ON ol.order_id = lo.order_id), prevp AS (SELECT tr.order_id, ol.product_id FROM tr JOIN ol ON ol.order_id = tr.prev_order_id), added AS (SELECT nl.order_id, nl.product_id FROM tr JOIN ol nl ON nl.order_id = tr.order_id LEFT JOIN prevp p ON p.order_id = nl.order_id AND p.product_id = nl.product_id WHERE p.order_id IS NULL), padd AS (SELECT product_id, count(*) AS n_add FROM added WHERE product_id IN (SELECT product_id FROM cand) GROUP BY product_id), qn AS (SELECT product_id AS seed_id, count(*) AS n_q FROM prevp WHERE product_id IN (SELECT seed_id FROM seeds) GROUP BY product_id), qp AS (SELECT p.product_id AS seed_id, a.product_id, count(*) AS n_qp FROM prevp p JOIN added a ON a.order_id = p.order_id WHERE p.product_id IN (SELECT seed_id FROM seeds) AND a.product_id IN (SELECT product_id FROM cand) GROUP BY p.product_id, a.product_id), sc AS (SELECT c.user_id, c.product_id, avg(COALESCE(qp.n_qp, 0) / (qn.n_q + 5.0)) AS p_add FROM cand c JOIN seeds s ON s.user_id = c.user_id AND s.seed_id <> c.product_id JOIN qn ON qn.seed_id = s.seed_id LEFT JOIN qp ON qp.seed_id = s.seed_id AND qp.product_id = c.product_id GROUP BY c.user_id, c.product_id) SELECT sc.user_id, sc.product_id, sc.p_add AS f_x_c3_next_add_prob_tw, ln((sc.p_add + 0.0001) / ((COALESCE(pa.n_add, 0) + 1.0) / (n.n_tr + 1.0) + 0.0001)) AS f_x_c3_next_add_lift_tw FROM sc LEFT JOIN padd pa ON pa.product_id = sc.product_id CROSS JOIN ntr n

rival.explanation: The lift may only pick up products with rising adoption (new launches, promotions) that get added after almost any basket, independent of the specific seed.
rival.stratum: Candidates with high p_trend or high ag_p_new_buyer_share

cards.name: user_knn_neighbourhood
cards.mechanism: User-user neighbourhood collaborative filtering. Each user's seeds are their 15 most-ordered products in the last 56 days among products with 2..300 distinct buyers, which are the distinctive tastes. Neighbours are other users sharing at least 2 seeds, with similarity sum(1/ln(1+buyers)); the top 50 are kept. The columns are the similarity-weighted share of neighbours who bought the candidate in the last 28 days, and its log lift over the global 28-day buyer share. Users with the same niche tastes (diet, household type, local assortment) buy similar new items. This lifts non-repeat candidates above plain popularity.
cards.stratum: Never-bought candidates of users with a broad recent repertoire. Predicate: NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.product_id = c.product_id) AND (SELECT count(DISTINCT l.product_id) FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 56 DAY) >= 20
cards.null_stratum: Users with almost no recent repertoire (few or no neighbours). Predicate: (SELECT count(DISTINCT l.product_id) FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 56 DAY) < 5

cards.name: category_next_order_transition
cards.mechanism: A category-level sequential transition graph over consecutive orders of all users, with the next order in the last 14 days. For each category s in the user's latest order, it takes P(candidate's category in next order | s in previous order), excluding s equal to the candidate's category. The columns are the mean over the last-order categories and its log lift over the category's base next-order rate. This captures cross-category order dynamics: after a big fresh-produce order, the next is a household or beverage top-up; after baby food, diapers. It tells which category, and so which candidates, the next order turns to. It is not about the user's own category recency, which is already covered.

cards.null_stratum: Products without a category (value NULL). Predicate: NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lines l WHERE l.product_id = c.product_id AND l.master_category_id IS NOT NULL)

rival.explanation: Because the consecutive orders belong to the same user, the transition probability mostly reflects category co-purchase propensity of the same households (a static affinity), not order-to-order sequencing.

cards.name: within_category_pick_transition
cards.mechanism: A product-to-product transition matrix inside each category, built from all users' consecutive category purchases over 120 days. For each user and category, the orders that contain the category form a sequence. Each pair of consecutive category orders gives transitions q -> p between products of that category. For a candidate, the seeds are the products the user picked in their latest order containing the candidate's category. The columns are the smoothed mean P(next pick = p | previous pick = q), shrunk toward p's share of category picks, and its log lift over that share. The self-transition (q = p) encodes item loyalty. Cross transitions encode substitution flows: which brand or flavour people switch to from the user's current pick. So substitutes the user is likely to rotate into rise, and products people tend to abandon fall.
cards.stratum: Candidates in categories the user bought, where the user's latest category pick was a different product. Predicate: EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lines l JOIN lines m ON m.master_category_id = l.master_category_id WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND m.product_id = c.product_id AND l.product_id <> c.product_id)

cards.name: personal_cross_transition
cards.mechanism: A personal order-to-order transition graph from the user's own 120-day sequence. For each product q in the user's latest order, it counts how often the user's order right after an order with q contained the candidate p (q != p). This is smoothed toward the user's base rate of p in non-first orders. The columns are the mean over q and the log lift over that base rate. Individual rotation habits (alternating two flavours, buying detergent the order after a big fresh order, a weekly-biweekly rhythm between product groups) make p predictable from what was just bought. Aggregate counts and the self-history columns miss this.

cards.null_stratum: Users with only 2 orders, where no personal pattern can be estimated. Predicate: (SELECT count(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = c.user_id) <= 2

rival.explanation: p_tr is mostly a smoothed version of the user's share of orders with p (up_share), so any gain is extra frequency information, not sequencing.
rival.stratum: Heavy users (u_orders >= 10) where up_share is already precise

cards.name: personal_self_markov
cards.mechanism: A first-order Markov chain of the candidate's presence in the user's own order sequence, starting from the first purchase in the 120-day window. It estimates P(in next | in current) and P(in next | not in current), smoothed toward the user's post-adoption base rate. The first column is the probability for the current state, i.e. whether p was in the latest order. The second is the persistence gap P(in|in) - P(in|out). A negative gap marks alternating products, which skip after being bought (stock-ups, rotation). A positive gap marks products that come in runs. Share and streak features cannot distinguish 'bought in half the orders, alternating' from 'bought in half the orders, in blocks'. For the next order these imply opposite predictions given the last state.
cards.stratum: Candidates bought at least 3 times by users with at least 6 orders in the window. Predicate: (SELECT count(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = c.user_id) >= 6 AND (SELECT count(DISTINCT l.order_id) FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.product_id = c.product_id) >= 3
cards.null_stratum: Candidates bought once, where the chain is just the prior. Predicate: (SELECT count(DISTINCT l.order_id) FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.product_id = c.product_id) = 1
cards.sql: WITH uo AS (SELECT user_id, order_id, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts, order_id) AS k, count(*) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id) AS n_ord FROM orders WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users)), up AS (SELECT DISTINCT uo.user_id, l.product_id, uo.k FROM lines l JOIN uo ON uo.order_id = l.order_id JOIN cand c ON c.user_id = uo.user_id AND c.product_id = l.product_id), fk AS (SELECT user_id, product_id, min(k) AS k_first FROM up GROUP BY user_id, product_id), g AS (SELECT f.user_id, f.product_id, uo.k, uo.n_ord, CASE WHEN up.k IS NULL THEN 0 ELSE 1 END AS inn FROM fk f JOIN uo ON uo.user_id = f.user_id AND uo.k >= f.k_first LEFT JOIN up ON up.user_id = f.user_id AND up.product_id = f.product_id AND up.k = uo.k), t AS (SELECT user_id, product_id, k, n_ord, inn, lead(inn) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id, product_id ORDER BY k) AS nxt FROM g), agg AS (SELECT user_id, product_id, sum(CASE WHEN inn = 1 AND nxt IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS n1, sum(CASE WHEN inn = 1 AND nxt = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS n11, sum(CASE WHEN inn = 0 AND nxt IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS n0, sum(CASE WHEN inn = 0 AND nxt = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS n01, max(CASE WHEN k = n_ord THEN inn ELSE 0 END) AS cur, avg(nxt) AS base FROM t GROUP BY user_id, product_id) SELECT user_id, product_id, CASE WHEN cur = 1 THEN (n11 + 2.0 * COALESCE(base, 0.3)) / (n1 + 2.0) ELSE (n01 + 2.0 * COALESCE(base, 0.3)) / (n0 + 2.0) END AS f_x_c3_self_markov_cur, (n11 + 1.0) / (n1 + 2.0) - (n01 + 1.0) / (n0 + 2.0) AS f_x_c3_self_markov_gap FROM agg

rival.explanation: The current-state column is close to ag_up_adopt_share combined with up_in_last_order, so any gain comes from a better-smoothed adoption share rather than from the Markov structure.
rival.stratum: Candidates with up_in_last_order = 1 and short purchase histories (2-3 orders)

cards.name: session_knn_next_order
cards.mechanism: Session-based nearest neighbours. The user's latest order is the query session. Its seeds are its 8 most distinctive products (2..300 orders with a following order in the last 56 days). Neighbour sessions are other users' orders from the last 56 days that contain the seeds, with similarity sum(1/ln(1+degree)); the top 50 are kept. The score of a candidate is the similarity-weighted share of those neighbours whose next order contained it, plus its log lift over the base rate of that product in next orders. People whose basket looked like this user's last basket reveal what tends to come next. This multi-step path (seed -> similar session -> its successor -> product) differs from user-level kNN and from item-level transitions.
cards.stratum: Users whose latest order has at least 3 niche products (<= 300 orders in 56 days), for candidates outside that order. Predicate: (SELECT count(*) FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.ts = (SELECT max(o.ts) AS last_ts FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = c.user_id) AND l.product_id IN (SELECT m.product_id FROM lines m WHERE m.ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 56 DAY GROUP BY m.product_id HAVING count(DISTINCT m.order_id) <= 300)) >= 3
cards.null_stratum: Users whose latest order has only mainstream products (no seeds, value NULL). Predicate: NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.ts = (SELECT max(o.ts) AS last_ts FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = c.user_id) AND l.product_id IN (SELECT m.product_id FROM lines m WHERE m.ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 56 DAY GROUP BY m.product_id HAVING count(DISTINCT m.order_id) <= 300))

rival.explanation: Neighbour sessions share the user's store or retailer and its niche assortment, so the score measures local assortment popularity rather than what comes after a similar basket.
rival.stratum: Users with u_main_share = 1 at small retailers, and candidates with high ag_ps_lift

cards.name: retailer_sale_silence
cards.mechanism: The base never asks whether a candidate is still on sale where the user shops. A repeat candidate last bought weeks ago may have been delisted or be out of stock at the user's main retailer, and nothing in the base separates that from an ordinary lapse. The family measures days since the product last sold at the user's main retailer (by 120-day order count), plus that silence times its usual sale-day frequency there, which is the expected number of missed sale days. A product that usually sells every day and has been silent for a week is effectively gone, so its rank should fall. A low-volume product that is silent for the same time is not unusual. Shelf-fresh old favourites move up.
cards.stratum: Repeat candidates not bought for 28+ days, and tail products at the main retailer: EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.product_id = c.product_id) AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.product_id = c.product_id AND l.ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY)
cards.null_stratum: Products that sold on almost every day of the last 4 weeks: (SELECT count(DISTINCT CAST(l.ts AS DATE)) FROM lines l WHERE l.product_id = c.product_id AND l.ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY) >= 27
cards.sql: WITH uo AS (SELECT o.user_id, o.retailer, count(*) AS n_o, max(o.ts) AS last_ts FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users) GROUP BY o.user_id, o.retailer), um AS (SELECT user_id, retailer FROM (SELECT user_id, retailer, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY n_o DESC, last_ts DESC, retailer) AS rn FROM uo) x WHERE rn = 1), rp AS (SELECT o.retailer, l.product_id, count(DISTINCT CAST(l.ts AS DATE)) AS n_days, max(l.ts) AS last_ts FROM lines l JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = l.order_id WHERE l.ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 90 DAY AND o.retailer IN (SELECT retailer FROM um) AND l.product_id IN (SELECT product_id FROM cand) GROUP BY o.retailer, l.product_id) SELECT c.user_id, c.product_id, COALESCE(epoch(TIMESTAMP '{A}' - rp.last_ts) / 86400.0, 90.0) AS f_x_c4_ret_silence_days, epoch(TIMESTAMP '{A}' - rp.last_ts) / 86400.0 * rp.n_days / 90.0 AS f_x_c4_ret_silence_exp FROM cand c JOIN um ON um.user_id = c.user_id LEFT JOIN rp ON rp.retailer = um.retailer AND rp.product_id = c.product_id;

rival.stratum: Never-bought candidates from the pop-retailer source with popr_rank > 50, for every kind of user

cards.name: new_user_second_order
cards.mechanism: For users with 1 to 3 orders, almost every pair column is NULL or near zero, so ranking falls back on population popularity. That is the wrong prior, because newcomers keep and add products differently from settled users. Newcomers are users whose first visible order is at or after A-90d, so they had no orders in the 30 days before. For them the family gives a smoothed P(product in order 2 | product in order 1), meaning what newcomers keep, and the rate at which the product appears in order 2 without being in order 1, meaning what newcomers add. Both predict the next order of short-history users better than overall reorder or adoption rates.
cards.stratum: Users with at most 3 orders in the visible window: (SELECT count(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = c.user_id) <= 3
cards.null_stratum: Settled users with long histories: (SELECT count(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = c.user_id) >= 10
cards.sql: WITH uf AS (SELECT user_id, min(ts) AS first_ts FROM orders GROUP BY user_id), nu AS (SELECT o.user_id, o.order_id, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY o.user_id ORDER BY o.ts, o.order_id) AS k FROM orders o JOIN uf ON uf.user_id = o.user_id WHERE uf.first_ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 90 DAY), o12 AS (SELECT user_id, max(CASE WHEN k = 1 THEN order_id END) AS o1, max(CASE WHEN k = 2 THEN order_id END) AS o2 FROM nu WHERE k <= 2 GROUP BY user_id HAVING count(*) = 2), p1 AS (SELECT DISTINCT o12.user_id, l.product_id FROM lines l JOIN o12 ON l.order_id = o12.o1), p2 AS (SELECT DISTINCT o12.user_id, l.product_id FROM lines l JOIN o12 ON l.order_id = o12.o2), nn AS (SELECT count(*) AS n_users FROM o12), pa AS (SELECT COALESCE(p1.product_id, p2.product_id) AS product_id, count(p1.user_id) AS n1, count(CASE WHEN p1.user_id IS NOT NULL AND p2.user_id IS NOT NULL THEN 1 END) AS n12, count(CASE WHEN p1.user_id IS NULL THEN 1 END) AS n2new FROM p1 FULL OUTER JOIN p2 ON p1.user_id = p2.user_id AND p1.product_id = p2.product_id GROUP BY COALESCE(p1.product_id, p2.product_id)), gr AS (SELECT sum(n12) * 1.0 / GREATEST(sum(n1), 1) AS r0 FROM pa), ap AS (SELECT DISTINCT product_id FROM lines) SELECT ap.product_id, (COALESCE(pa.n12, 0) + 5.0 * gr.r0) / (COALESCE(pa.n1, 0) + 5.0) AS f_x_c4_p_newu_keep, (COALESCE(pa.n2new, 0) + 0.1) / (nn.n_users - COALESCE(pa.n1, 0) + 1.0) AS f_x_c4_p_newu_adopt FROM ap LEFT JOIN pa ON pa.product_id = ap.product_id CROSS JOIN gr CROSS JOIN nn;

rival.explanation: The adopt column may just be a generic trial propensity (products pushed in newcomer promotions or onboarding bundles), so it would help never-bought candidates for every user, not only newcomers.
rival.stratum: Never-bought candidates of users with 4+ orders

cards.name: price_tier_fit
cards.mechanism: Popularity candidates for users with little product overlap are ranked only by counts, but users have a stable price tier: budget versus premium choices within a category. The family computes each product's log median price relative to its category's median product price over 28 days. It then measures the gap between the candidate's index and the user's mean index over all their lines, and the gap to the user's mean index within the candidate's category. Never-bought candidates in the user's tier should rank above off-tier popular items.

cards.null_stratum: Established repeat candidates: (SELECT count(DISTINCT l.order_id) FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.product_id = c.product_id) >= 3

cards.name: staple_far_copurchase
cards.mechanism: Existing co-purchase signals are seeded only by the latest order. Candidates related to the user's long-run staples that happened to be missing from the last basket are therefore described poorly. The seeds are the user's top 3 multi-order products that were not in the latest order. Over the last 7 days the family gives the mean smoothed P(candidate in an order | seed in that order) and its log lift over the candidate's base rate. This links far-from-latest repeat candidates and never-bought complements to the user's stable habits.

cards.mechanism: Repeat candidates far from the latest interactions (up_days_since_last > 28) are the hardest repeat group. The family measures the smoothed share of the user's repurchases that came after a gap of 28+ days since the previous purchase of the same product. It also gives the user's median product rebuy gap. cards.mechanism: Users coming back after a long pause (21+ days since their previous order) are poorly served. cards.name: retailer_shelf_age
cards.mechanism: Cold items are described poorly. A product that appeared at the user's main retailer only recently has low 28-day counts, NULL repeat statistics and no history with the user, even if it is selling fast. The family gives days since the product's first sale at the user's main retailer within the visible window. It also gives the signed days between that first sale and the user's last order: positive means the product is new on the shelf since the user's last visit, so the user has not yet had a chance to try it. These separate fresh launches from long-ignored items with the same low counts.
cards.stratum: Products first sold at the user's main retailer within the last 28 days, users not seen in the last week: (SELECT min(l.ts) FROM lines l JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = l.order_id WHERE l.product_id = c.product_id AND o.retailer = (SELECT mode(o2.retailer) FROM orders o2 WHERE o2.user_id = c.user_id)) >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY
cards.null_stratum: Products sold at the retailer since the start of the visible window: (SELECT min(l.ts) FROM lines l WHERE l.product_id = c.product_id) < TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 110 DAY
cards.sql: WITH uo AS (SELECT o.user_id, o.retailer, count(*) AS n_o, max(o.ts) AS last_ts FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users) GROUP BY o.user_id, o.retailer), um AS (SELECT user_id, retailer FROM (SELECT user_id, retailer, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY n_o DESC, last_ts DESC, retailer) AS rn FROM uo) x WHERE rn = 1), ul AS (SELECT user_id, max(last_ts) AS last_ts FROM uo GROUP BY user_id), rf AS (SELECT o.retailer, l.product_id, min(l.ts) AS first_ts FROM lines l JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = l.order_id WHERE o.retailer IN (SELECT retailer FROM um) AND l.product_id IN (SELECT product_id FROM cand) GROUP BY o.retailer, l.product_id) SELECT c.user_id, c.product_id, epoch(TIMESTAMP '{A}' - rf.first_ts) / 86400.0 AS f_x_c4_ret_age_days, epoch(rf.first_ts - ul.last_ts) / 86400.0 AS f_x_c4_new_since_visit FROM cand c JOIN um ON um.user_id = c.user_id JOIN ul ON ul.user_id = c.user_id LEFT JOIN rf ON rf.retailer = um.retailer AND rf.product_id = c.product_id;

twin.sql: WITH uo AS (SELECT o.user_id, o.retailer, count(*) AS n_o, max(o.ts) AS last_ts FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users) GROUP BY o.user_id, o.retailer), um AS (SELECT user_id, retailer FROM (SELECT user_id, retailer, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY n_o DESC, last_ts DESC, retailer) AS rn FROM uo) x WHERE rn = 1), ul AS (SELECT user_id, max(last_ts) AS last_ts FROM uo GROUP BY user_id), rf AS (SELECT o.retailer, l.product_id, arg_min(l.ts, hash(l.order_id, l.line_item_id)) AS first_ts FROM lines l JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = l.order_id WHERE o.retailer IN (SELECT retailer FROM um) AND l.product_id IN (SELECT product_id FROM cand) GROUP BY o.retailer, l.product_id) SELECT c.user_id, c.product_id, epoch(TIMESTAMP '{A}' - rf.first_ts) / 86400.0 AS f_x_c4_ret_age_days_tw, epoch(rf.first_ts - ul.last_ts) / 86400.0 AS f_x_c4_new_since_visit_tw FROM cand c JOIN um ON um.user_id = c.user_id JOIN ul ON ul.user_id = c.user_id LEFT JOIN rf ON rf.retailer = um.retailer AND rf.product_id = c.product_id;

rival.explanation: Shelf age may proxy launch promotions (new products are discounted and featured), so the gain would coincide with the promo columns instead of with the user's missed exposure.
rival.stratum: Candidates with a positive 7-day discount share (ag_p_promo7 > 0), for all users
